subject: Biotechnology
title: Justice and Access in Biotech
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Justice and Access in Biotech.

hook.text: Gene therapy costs $2 million per patient — who gets treated when only the wealthy can afford a cure?

buildup.text: Distributive justice asks how biotech benefits should be shared — equally, by need, or by ability to pay?

discovery.text: TRIPS agreements protect biotech patents globally — developing nations cannot afford patented medicines or seeds.

twist.text: Compulsory licensing lets countries override patents during emergencies — India manufactures generic HIV drugs for Africa.

climax.text: Outcome-based pricing ties payment to whether a gene therapy works — Novartis only charges if Zolgensma cures the patient.

punchline.text: Innovation without access is not progress — bioethics demands benefits reach everyone.

quiz.question: What is compulsory licensing in the context of biotech patents?
options: A requirement that all biotech products must be licensed before sale
A legal mechanism allowing countries to override patents to manufacture affordable generic versions during emergencies
A system where companies must license their technology to competitors for free

details.summary: Biotechnology breakthroughs often reach wealthy populations first, creating health and agricultural divides. Gene therapies costing millions, patented seeds, and personalized medicine raise justice concerns about who benefits from publicly funded scientific research.
details.whyItMatters: If biotechnology only serves those who can afford it, existing inequalities deepen. Ensuring equitable access to biotech advances is essential for the technology to fulfill its promise of improving health and food security for all.
takeaways: Gene therapies can cost over two million dollars per treatment
Patent systems can restrict access to life-saving biotech innovations
Public funding of research raises questions about public access to results

faq.question: Why are gene therapies so expensive?
faq.answer: Gene therapies require complex personalized manufacturing, extensive quality testing, and treat small patient populations that cannot generate economies of scale. Development costs are spread over few patients. New manufacturing approaches and larger markets may reduce prices over time.

faq.question: How can biotech benefits be made more equitable?
faq.answer: Strategies include tiered pricing for different countries, compulsory licensing for essential medicines, open-source biotech initiatives, public-private partnerships, and ensuring developing countries can build domestic biotech capacity rather than depending on imports.
